title: Remy and Cobble's Sunny Surprise
markdown:
The farmyard was usually a busy place of clucks and moos and oinks. This morning it was quiet. Too quiet. The sky was a deep inky blue, the sort you see late at night, though it ought to have worn the first rosy blush of dawn. The whole world seemed to be holding its breath.

Remy the rooster, alarm clock for miles around, said nothing. His feathers were the brightest red you ever did see, and his crow could shake the barn. He had a secret, though. He was super, super scared of the dark. In the dark his heart went thump-thump-thump, fast as a drum. Wobbly shadows stretched longer than they should. He thought he heard whispers in the eaves. Colours felt as if they had been packed away in a box with no lid he dared open. This dim morning felt like his old worry had spilled over the whole farm.

The sleepy sheep stayed in fluffy heaps. The hens huddled wing to wing. The cheerful pigs snoozed soundlessly in their straw, as if even oinking had been postponed. It was as if the world had forgotten how to wake.

Cobble was not your usual farm resident. He was a cobweb wizard, no bigger than a thumb, with shiny thin threads he could make appear and disappear. Usually those threads mended a tiny tear in a hen’s feather, or made a dewdrop sparkle. He was quiet, and often felt as invisible as silk between blades of grass. Today even Cobble felt the strangeness.

Remy paced by the barn. His bright comb drooped. “Cock-a-doodle-doo-waiiit. Where is it?” His voice was a shaky whisper. “The sun. It’s gone. What if it never comes back?” A cold pebble settled in his chest.

Cobble, perched on a fence post, wiggled his tiny eight-legged toes. “Perhaps,” he squeaked, “something has happened to it.”

Remy jumped, tail feathers puffing. “Happened? To the sun?” He pictured grumpy clouds gobbling it, or giant hands snatching it away.

Cobble felt a small ember of determination. “I think we should go and look. Somewhere. Everywhere.” He almost added, even if it is dark, and then did not, because he could see Remy’s knees.

Remy fluffed, trying to sound brave. “Look? Out there? In all this darkness?” He wanted the coop. He looked at Cobble, so small and so ready. “All right, Cobble. We’ll look. But you stay close. Very, very close. And if you see a shadow that looks like a particularly grumpy badger, you tell me at once.”

They stepped into the deeper gloom beyond the barn door, Remy’s claws clicking softer than usual.

The farmyard was not only dark. It was full of sleepers. They tiptoed past Cadi the bull, who snored like rumbling thunder that vibrated through the earth, his great sides rising and falling like a weather system. They eased around hens who might peck anything that moved with a sharp surprised peck. Cobble’s eyes were bright beads in the dim, and he whispered like a secret agent. “Left, Remy, past the watering trough. Don’t step on that grumpy toad. Mind the sleepy cat curled by the door. She dreams of chasing mice, but she might chase a rooster too.”

Remy held his breath past Cadi’s stall. One eye of the bull half-opened, then closed again, as if dawn were a rumour he refused to believe.

Next came the rickety barn ladder. Each step groaned. Remy’s feathers ruffled. “Oh, feathers and dust,” he clucked, scanning the inky black. He pictured the ladder crumbling and a tumble into a pile of forgotten hay. Cobble had a clever glimmer. He spun his strongest, shiniest threads, hitching them to the rungs and to Remy’s spurs. “Hold on tight,” he chirped, a confident hum in the small voice. The threads felt surprisingly strong, like invisible ropes woven from leftover moonlight, guiding the climb and offering extra grip. Remy went up one rung, then another, Cobble a silver spark at his shoulder.

When they finally reached the top of the barn and peered out over the silent dark farm, they saw it. It was truly extraordinary, a sight that made Remy forget his fear for a moment. Tied to the very peak of the barn roof, where the wind usually played tag with the weather vane, was the sunrise. Not the sun itself, but the golden shimmering glow that signals its arrival, a beautiful captive dawn. It was caught, tethered by a thick rainbow-coloured string, and it pulsed weakly, unable to break free, like a trapped butterfly trying to fly.

Remy gasped, beak falling open. “It’s… it’s tied up.”

Cobble, looking at the pulsing light, understood at once. Someone, or something, had tied the sunrise to keep the farm in darkness, to stop the day from beginning. “We have to free it, Remy.” His shyness had melted away like dew.

Suddenly a gust of wind swept through the farmyard, whistling around the barn. It rattled the old roof tiles and shook the tethered sunrise, making it bob precariously. The rainbow string quivered, and Remy, with his sharp rooster eyes, saw a strand of it fray, thin and weak. The darkness seemed to press in even harder, as if trying to smother the last bits of light.

He was so high. The dark was so deep. The string looked so fragile. He imagined it snapping and the sunrise vanishing into endless night. His knees offered to buckle. He wanted to close his eyes, bury his head in his feathers, and wish himself back to the safety of the coop. The old fear washed through him, cold as well-water.

Cobble’s small voice cut the wind. “Remy. Remember your crow. Your voice is strong. It can shake the world.” He was right. Remy’s crow was the sound of morning, the sound that chased lingering shadows. Cobble was already spinning more threads, weaving them with desperate focused energy, his tiny body a blur. Remy took a deep breath of cool night air. He was not going to let the worry win. Not today. Not when the sunrise needed him.

He looked at Cobble, then at the pulsing gold. He puffed his chest as big as a barn door would allow. He opened his beak and crowed with everything in him.

“Cock-a-doodle-doo.”

The sound was not only loud. It was morning, poured out on purpose. The old roof creaked. The fraying string sang along. Cobble’s threads held the thin places. Together — the thunderous crow across the silent fields and the little wizard’s stitching — they were too much for the flimsy tether.

With a final mighty snap, the rainbow tether broke. The sunrise, now free, leaped into the sky, blazing with all its golden glory, like a triumphant banner unfurling.

And there it was. Light. Warm, bright, glorious light flooded the farmyard, chasing away every shadow, every doubt. Remy stood on the rooftop, his comb held high, his magnificent feathers catching the new light, no longer folded small. He looked at the farm below, bathed in sunshine. Sheep blinked. Hens muttered the first proper clucks of the day. Cadi the bull gave one last thunderous snore and then a surprised huff, as if day had tapped him on the nose. Cobble, tired but beaming, settled onto Remy’s comb, his delicate threads catching the new light and sparkling like tiny jewels. Remy crowed once more, just to be sure, and this time the dark did not answer back. The weather vane, free of the rainbow string, turned a slow happy circle in the morning wind.
characters: Remy (a rooster afraid of the dark), Cobble (a cobweb wizard)
